section_summary: This section consists chiefly of protests from private citizens, churches, missionary societies, and peace organizations urging the United States to embargo arms, oil, scrap metal, and other supplies shipped to Japan during the Sino-Japanese War. State Department replies repeatedly explain that the Neutrality Act could be invoked only after a presidential finding of war, would then apply equally to China and Japan, and did not authorize restrictions on raw materials; several replies also cite arms-export license totals and condemn civilian bombing. The section additionally addresses protection and recovery of American missionary property in China and concludes with a Moscow Embassy despatch transmitting a Soviet newspaper article accusing American financial and industrial interests of sustaining Japanese aggression.

subfiles.title: Continuation of State Department reply on arms exports to China and Japan
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains why the administration has not invoked the Neutrality Act against China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The continuation argues that no legal authority exists to prevent arms exports without a presidential proclamation recognizing a state of war. It states that broader national interests counsel against invoking the act and reports arms-export licenses worth approximately $14.27 million for China and $10.72 million for Japan since July 1, 1937.

subfiles.title: John Oliver letter urging enforcement of neutrality
subfiles.from: John Oliver
subfiles.about: Urges the government to halt shipments of war materials to Japan, China, and Spain.
subfiles.summary: Oliver condemns shipments of gasoline and oil allegedly loaded from an offshore pipeline near San Luis Obispo for delivery to Japan. Invoking humanity, he asks Hull to enforce neutrality and stop American commerce from sustaining war.

subfiles.title: Reply to John Oliver
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the legal treatment of exports to Spain, China, and Japan under neutrality legislation.
subfiles.summary: The reply notes that arms exports to Spain are already prohibited but that no presidential proclamation has made the Neutrality Act applicable to China and Japan. It further explains that gasoline and oil are not legally classified as arms and that no statute authorizes their prohibition, while defending the President's decision not to invoke the joint resolution.

subfiles.title: Buffalo Methodist district superintendent's covering letter
subfiles.from: Mr. Koen, District Superintendent, Buffalo District
subfiles.about: Forwards a district conference resolution opposing American support for Japan's invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: The superintendent states that the Buffalo District's conference, representing sixty-five Methodist churches, adopted the enclosed resolution on September 20. He asks the Secretary of State to consider its two principal requests.

subfiles.title: Resolution for Withholding American Cooperation in the Invasion of China
subfiles.from: District Conference, Buffalo District, Methodist Episcopal Church
subfiles.to: President and Government of the United States
subfiles.about: Calls for restrictions on American resources used by Japan and material assistance to China.
subfiles.summary: The resolution alleges that American exports supply a majority of Japan's imported war materials. It urges restrictions on scrap iron, oil, aviation gasoline, and financial resources, and requests a substantial wheat-and-cotton loan to China.

subfiles.title: Reply to the Buffalo District superintendent
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to the Buffalo Methodist resolution concerning the Far East.
subfiles.summary: The Department explains that a presidential war proclamation would prohibit arms exports to both China and Japan, while no authority permits a unilateral embargo on Japan. It defends non-invocation of the Neutrality Act, notes that nonmilitary commodities cannot be restricted under it, and supplies comparative arms-license totals.

subfiles.title: Carter's Ink Company letter to the President
subfiles.from: Mr. Carter, Carter's Ink Company
subfiles.about: Protests continued American furnishing of munitions to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The writer describes American sympathy for China and condemnation of Japan as nearly universal. He argues that governmental inability to stop munitions exports would justify pessimism and disgust.

subfiles.title: Carter's Ink Company letter to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: Mr. Carter, Carter's Ink Company
subfiles.about: Repeats the protest against American munitions shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: This letter closely duplicates the appeal sent to the President. It contends that Japan could not continue the war without American munitions and criticizes the government for failing to act.

subfiles.title: Reply to Mr. Carter
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Answers Carter's two letters concerning exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that the Neutrality Act would operate only after a presidential proclamation and would then bar arms exports to China as well as Japan. It says that nonmilitary commodities cannot be embargoed under existing law and reports licensed arms-export values for the two countries.

subfiles.title: New Haven Conference of Youth covering letter
subfiles.from: William Post
subfiles.about: Forwards an embargo resolution adopted by five hundred people in New Haven.
subfiles.summary: Post reports that the resolution was passed at a meeting in the New Haven Y.W.C.A. on the preceding day. He asks Hull to give the proposed embargo prompt attention.

subfiles.title: New Haven Conference of Youth Resolution on China
subfiles.from: Five hundred attendees at the New Haven Y.W.C.A.
subfiles.to: Franklin D. Roosevelt and Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Demands a complete embargo against Japan until its forces withdraw from China.
subfiles.summary: The resolution identifies the United States as Japan's chief supplier of scrap iron, oil, high-test gasoline, and other war materials and labels Japan the aggressor. It calls for an embargo covering arms, ammunition, gasoline, and raw materials until Japan withdraws from China.

subfiles.title: Reply to William Post
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to the New Haven embargo resolution.
subfiles.summary: The Department explains that the Neutrality Act cannot be applied without a presidential war proclamation and could not discriminate between China and Japan. It also states that the law does not cover ordinary raw materials and cites licensed arms-export totals for both countries.

subfiles.title: Mrs. William Ruhl Clymer follow-up letter
subfiles.from: Mrs. William Ruhl Clymer
subfiles.about: Thanks Yost for an earlier explanation and reflects on the need for an adaptable foreign policy.
subfiles.summary: Clymer acknowledges that her earlier questions fell outside existing neutrality legislation but hopes to influence policy before Congress reconvenes in January. Referring to rapidly changing events and the meeting of the Big Four, she expresses cautious hope that fewer arms will require governmental control.

subfiles.title: White House memorandum requesting a draft reply
subfiles.from: Franklin D. Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Requests preparation of a reply to Rockwell Kent for the President's signature.
subfiles.summary: The White House refers Kent's protest to the State Department. Roosevelt asks that a response be drafted for his approval and signature.

subfiles.title: Rockwell Kent protest to President Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Rockwell Kent
subfiles.about: Protests the administration's permitting shipments of arms and supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Kent argues that the administration's policy misrepresents the wishes of its own supporters and makes the United States complicit in wars of conquest. Although identifying himself as a staunch supporter, he warns that continued assistance to aggressors will cost the administration popular backing.

subfiles.title: Hull transmittal of draft reply to Rockwell Kent
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Sends the President a proposed response to Kent's protest.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that the draft was prepared in compliance with Roosevelt's October 13 memorandum. He encloses the proposed letter and Kent's original correspondence for presidential action.

subfiles.title: Draft presidential reply to Rockwell Kent
subfiles.from: Franklin D. Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Explains the statutory limits on presidential authority over exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The draft says a neutrality proclamation would have to affect both China and Japan and that oil, scrap iron, and similar commodities fall outside the legal definition of arms. It cites arms-license figures, mentions advisory efforts to discourage exports that encourage civilian bombing, and thanks Kent for supporting the administration's general policies.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Graham Wilson request and neutrality protest
subfiles.from: Mrs. Graham Wilson
subfiles.about: Requests copies of the neutrality law and protests its nonapplication to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Wilson asks for several copies of the Neutrality Act. Although approving of peace statements and trade agreements, she says she cannot understand the failure to apply the law to Japanese actions in China.

subfiles.title: Reply to Mrs. Graham Wilson
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Supplies copies of the neutrality resolution and explains why it has not been invoked.
subfiles.summary: The reply emphasizes that a presidential proclamation would impose an arms embargo equally on China and Japan and that the President has judged invocation contrary to broader national interests. It notes that the act cannot restrict other commodities and provides comparative arms-export license totals.

subfiles.title: Hatherly Methodist Episcopal Church appeal
subfiles.from: Wesley H. McPhee and Royer H. Woodburn for the Official Board
subfiles.about: Urges the government to stop exports of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The church officials argue that American scrap iron, oil, and other materials sustain Japanese aggression in Asia. They believe the administration could exert sufficient power and pressure to help end the war.

subfiles.title: Reply to the Hatherly Methodist Episcopal Church
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Wesley H. McPhee and the Official Board
subfiles.about: Answers the church's request for restrictions on exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department repeats that the Neutrality Act requires a presidential proclamation and would apply to both belligerents. It states that the law cannot control commodities outside the statutory arms list and gives arms-license totals for China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Dwenger letter concerning trade and shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: Mrs. Dwenger
subfiles.about: Comments favorably on trade agreements while objecting to American materials reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: The handwritten letter is badly degraded in the OCR, but the subsequent reply identifies its subject as shipments of materials to Japan. It also evidently praises the administration's trade-agreements program and asks what action can be taken under existing law.

subfiles.title: Reply to Mrs. Dwenger
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains neutrality policy in response to concerns about shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department thanks Dwenger for her favorable comments on trade agreements and explains that no arms embargo is possible without a presidential finding of war. It adds that nonmilitary commodities are beyond the Neutrality Act's scope and reports arms-export license totals for China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Trinity Union Methodist Episcopal Church appeal
subfiles.from: Edward M. Wheeler, Recording Steward
subfiles.about: Communicates a church conference's plea to end American war-sustaining trade with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Wheeler reports instructions from the church's October 11 Quarterly Conference. The church calls the traffic a form of American partnership in the Far Eastern conflict and urges Hull to help end the destruction of Chinese lives and property.

subfiles.title: Reply to Edward M. Wheeler
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to the Trinity Union Methodist Church's protest against exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department appreciates the church's views but reiterates that an arms embargo requires a presidential proclamation and must cover both China and Japan. It says other commodities cannot be prohibited under the Neutrality Act and furnishes current license totals.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on missionary property
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Department of State officials preparing a reply
subfiles.about: Suggests language concerning protection and recovery of American missionary property in China.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum says the government has protected American lives, protested damage to missionary and commercial interests, and reserved American claims arising from military operations. It reports successful recovery of missionary property at Yangzhou, Kunshan, and Suzhou through representations to Japanese authorities.

subfiles.title: Seminole Women's Missionary Society petition
subfiles.from: Mrs. Carlos Wear and other members of the Women's Missionary Society
subfiles.about: Opposes raw-material exports to Japan and Japanese confiscation of church property in China.
subfiles.summary: The signatories ask Hull to protest sales of cotton, oil, iron, and steel to Japan. They also request the return of confiscated church properties to their rightful owners and thank him for efforts to preserve peace.

subfiles.title: Reply to the Seminole Women's Missionary Society
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Mrs. Carlos Wear and fellow society members
subfiles.about: Addresses both raw-material exports and protection of missionary property in China.
subfiles.summary: The reply explains that cotton, oil, iron, and steel are excluded from the arms categories that the Neutrality Act permits the President to restrict. It describes diplomatic and consular procedures for protecting Americans and reports the recent recovery of missionary properties at Yangzhou, Kunshan, and Suzhou.

subfiles.title: Wisconsin Congregational Conference resolution letter
subfiles.from: Theo. R. Faville
subfiles.about: Transmits a unanimous church resolution opposing material assistance to Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: The resolution expresses sympathy with Christians and other people in both China and Japan while condemning the Japanese military group's war of aggression. It urges citizens, businesses, and government to stop selling Japan materials that sustain the conflict and acknowledges American responsibility for crises in Europe and Asia.

subfiles.title: Reply to Theo. R. Faville
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to the Wisconsin Congregational Conference resolution.
subfiles.summary: The Department thanks Faville for the resolution and explains that a neutrality proclamation would impose an embargo on both China and Japan. It defends the President's decision not to invoke the act, notes its limited commodity coverage, and supplies arms-export license figures.

subfiles.title: Connecticut Peace Conference covering letter
subfiles.from: Chase Kimball
subfiles.about: Forwards two resolutions adopted by attendees at a New Haven peace meeting.
subfiles.summary: Kimball explains that the resolutions represent the meeting's participants rather than formally binding the Connecticut Peace Conference or its member organizations. More than one hundred of 114 attendees supported the Japan resolution, while the disarmament resolution passed unanimously.

subfiles.title: Resolution supporting an international disarmament conference
subfiles.from: Attendees at the New Haven Y.W.C.A. meeting
subfiles.about: Supports American leadership in an international conference for economic and military disarmament.
subfiles.summary: The attendees endorse the administration's declared purpose of convening an international disarmament conference. They pledge support for American participation and for the political and economic measures needed to make such a conference successful.

subfiles.title: Resolution against American support for Japanese aggression
subfiles.from: Attendees at the New Haven Y.W.C.A. meeting
subfiles.to: President and Congress of the United States
subfiles.about: Petitions the government to end American trade sustaining Japan's war in China.
subfiles.summary: The resolution condemns Japan's treaty violations, bombing of Chinese cities, and attacks on civilian and foreign property, while cataloguing American exports used by Japanese forces. It asks for every practical measure to end the traffic and offers moral support to groups refusing to sell or ship war supplies to Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply to Chase Kimball
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Responds to the New Haven resolutions on disarmament and exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department repeats the statutory explanation that an arms embargo would require a presidential proclamation and would apply equally to China and Japan. It also states that other commodities lie outside the Neutrality Act, cites export-license totals, and notes that manufacturers have been directly informed of the government's condemnation of civilian bombing and its material encouragement.

subfiles.title: Senator Prentiss M. Brown referral letter
subfiles.from: Prentiss M. Brown
subfiles.about: Forwards a Detroit church letter and asks for information to use in replying.
subfiles.summary: Brown encloses a letter from the superintendent and pastor of Central Methodist Church concerning the war in China. He asks Hull to supply information upon which he may base his response and requests return of the original.

subfiles.title: Central Methodist Church letter to Senator Brown
subfiles.from: John D. Fatt and Oscar G. Starrett
subfiles.about: Provides the senator with the church's appeal concerning the war in China.
subfiles.summary: The page identifies the superintendent and pastor and states that the letter is exactly the same as their letter of the same date to the Secretary of State. It serves as the copy transmitted to Senator Brown for assistance.

subfiles.title: Central Methodist Church appeal to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: John D. Fatt, Oscar G. Starrett, and members of the Chinese Sunday School
subfiles.about: Urges action to stop American war materials and supplies from assisting Japan in China.
subfiles.summary: The writers describe relief contributions for China but argue that ending the conflict requires cutting Japan's supply of American ammunition, weapons, and fuel. They portray Japan as an aggressor and treaty breaker, call for international quarantine, and accuse the government of hypocrisy for condemning the bombing of Canton and Hankou while permitting trade that enables it. Two pages of additional signatures follow.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Brown
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Supplies the Department's response and supporting publications for the senator's information.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Brown's referral and encloses a copy of its reply to Fatt and Starrett. It also supplies the referenced pamphlet and Neutrality Act and returns the church's original letter as requested.

subfiles.title: Reply to John D. Fatt and Oscar G. Starrett
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green
subfiles.to: John D. Fatt and Oscar G. Starrett
subfiles.about: Explains the government's legal position on war-material exports and civilian bombing.
subfiles.summary: Green states that an arms embargo requires a presidential war proclamation, would apply to both China and Japan, and cannot cover commodities outside the statutory munitions list. He gives arms-license totals and adds that the government has repeatedly condemned civilian bombing and directly communicated that position to American aircraft and aeronautical-equipment exporters.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs summary of Moscow Despatch No. 1666
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Soviet article alleging American business support for Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum says the article portrays American financial and business interests as welcoming Japanese orders, favoring Japanese expansion at China's expense, and undermining the anti-Japanese boycott. It notes accusations that American oil and other assistance sustained Japan and that the Ford Company in Japan subscribed to a Japanese war loan.

subfiles.title: Moscow Embassy Despatch No. 1666
subfiles.from: A. C. Kirk, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Moscow
subfiles.about: Transmits the Russian text and English translation of an Izvestiya article on American support for Japan's war.
subfiles.summary: Kirk forwards K. Volkov's article “Wall Street and Japanese Aggression in China,” published on September 10. He explains that the article draws partly on American sources to argue that Japan's campaign in China depends heavily on sales of essential military commodities by American industrialists.

subfiles.title: Russian clipping of “Wall Street and Japanese Aggression in China”
subfiles.from: K. Volkov, Izvestiya
subfiles.to: Enclosure to Moscow Embassy Despatch No. 1666
subfiles.about: Presents the original Russian version of a Soviet critique of American economic assistance to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The clipping is the Russian-language source attached to the Moscow despatch, although the OCR preserves little usable Cyrillic text. Its argument, clarified by the memorandum and translation, is that American industrialists and financiers supplied strategic materials and capital essential to Japanese aggression in China.

subfiles.title: Translation of “Wall Street and Japanese Aggression in China”
subfiles.from: K. Volkov, translated by the American Embassy in Moscow
subfiles.about: Begins the English translation of the Soviet article criticizing American commercial support for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Volkov argues that American manufacturers and financiers directly and indirectly sustain Japan by supplying strategic raw materials and armaments, quoting Lenin on Japan's dependence upon foreign financial and military support. He contends that London and New York finance influence the war's outcome and cites George Bogen as evidence that American business circles accept Japanese economic expansion in northern China and Shanghai while resisting a boycott.
